Am I required to buy it?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside those zones, a lender may still require it.

In Florida, a home insured by Citizens Property Insurance with wind coverage must also carry flood insurance. In a high-risk zone (A or V) this has applied since 2023 (new policies from April 1, renewals from July 1), whatever the home is worth. Outside those zones it phases in by rebuilding cost: from January 1, 2026 at $400,000 or more, and from January 1, 2027 for all other Citizens homes. Condo-unit and no-wind policies are exempt.

Citizens does not sell flood insurance: the required flood policy comes from another insurer, the NFIP or a private one, and must at least match the NFIP's dwelling coverage or meet Florida's private flood insurance rules (s. 627.715).

At a closing: In Florida, a home seller must give the buyer a flood disclosure at or before the sales contract, saying whether the seller knows of flood damage during their ownership, filed a flood claim, or received flood aid (s. 689.302, F.S.).

81.9% of Gulf County's NFIP policy units are in high-risk zones. That is a share of insured policy units, not of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home.

Of the NFIP claim dollars paid here (1978–2024), 25.5% went to claims rated outside high-risk zones A and V. That uses the zone on each claim, not today's map, and leaves out claims with no zone.

Flood map: FEMA's current flood map for unincorporated Gulf County took effect March 9, 2021. FEMA's latest Community Status Book lists no new flood map taking effect for the towns and areas FEMA lists in this county; that does not cover maps still preliminary (below). FEMA's digital flood map for Gulf County has 93 map panels, the oldest in effect since March 9, 2021 and the newest since March 9, 2021. FEMA's map service lists no Letters of Map Revision on that map.

Owners here asked FEMA to take a building or lot out of the high-risk zone 243 times (rulings in FEMA's LOMA map layer):

  • 153 took the building or some or all of the lot out
  • 23 found it already outside the zone as mapped
  • 63 were denied
  • 4 were other or mixed

FEMA charges no review or processing fee for a Letter of Map Amendment request (44 CFR §72.5). FEMA's Online LOMC site lets home owners or their representatives ask FEMA for a Letter of Map Change. Your home may already have an Elevation Certificate on file with your community: ask your local floodplain manager, often in the city or county building, permitting or engineering department. If none is on file, a land surveyor, engineer or architect completes one.

These counts are for owners who applied, not your home's odds. FEMA's map service gives no dates for them. They are counted by the towns and areas FEMA lists in this county, so a city that reaches into a neighboring county counts in full here.

FEMA's preliminary flood map data give an early look at a home's or community's projected flood risk and may include new or revised flood maps. Check your own address on FEMA's flood map or with our flood zone map lookup by address.

Flood insurance cost in Gulf County, Florida

In Gulf County, single-family primary-home NFIP policies typically cost about $1,260 a year ($105 a month), fees included. Half pay between $1,035 and $1,920. To check a quote, use the checker at the top.

A quarter pay under $1,035 · Typical $1,260 · A quarter pay over $1,920 · A tenth pay $2,988 or more

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus the federal policy fee, reserve fund assessment and HFIAA surcharge), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half of policies, from 802 single-family primary-home policies. These are existing policies, many still below FEMA's full-risk price.

The NFIP also offers policies for renters and businesses. The median here is for single-family primary-home policies, not businesses or second homes. Renting? See what renters pay.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy. Bought while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, it can start at closing if the insurer is paid within 10 days (30 if the lender, title company or settlement attorney pays).

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageCan start at closing, if paid in time
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage. Does homeowners insurance cover flooding? To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim), and send a proof of loss (your signed, sworn statement of the amount you are claiming) within 60 days of the flood (44 CFR 61, App. A(1), Art. VII). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster.

Wait exceptions, exclusions, premium increases and surcharges, aid, appeals, rebuilding and closing rules: the NFIP rules in full.

Your state's insurance regulator: Florida Department of Financial Services (consumer help).

Source: floodsmart.gov, agents.floodsmart.gov, fema.gov, ecfr.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

Flood insurance claims in Gulf County, Florida: what floods pay out

Floods in Gulf County have led to 1,691 NFIP flood claims and $93.8 million in building and contents payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2018, 1995 and 2005.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2018 ($81,759,035), 1995 ($4,845,826), 2005 ($1,996,894). Total paid $93,838,437. How this is counted

Outside the high-risk zones: 999 claims here from losses 2016–2025 have a flood zone on the claim. Of these, 24.4% were rated outside zones A and V (zones X, B, C and D). They got 25.7% of the dollars paid on these claims. The zone is the one on each claim, not today's map; claims with no zone on them are left out.

Do flood claims here actually pay out?

Most do: 90.2% of claims in Gulf County paid something. The average paid claim was $62,048 (all years, in dollars of the day, not adjusted for inflation).

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for at least 37.6% of the 487 single-family policies here that report a rebuilding cost: FEMA's records put it above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 487 policies reporting one)37.6%Florida: 38.5%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)83.0%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 1,489 claims paid with a damage figure)7.9%

The two shares have different bases: insured-to-the-maximum counts every single-family policy with the full building limit; the rebuilding-cost share counts only the policies that report a rebuilding cost. Homes insured for less than their own rebuilding cost can also fall short. How this is counted

The NFIP pays the cost to rebuild (not a depreciated value) only for a single-family home that is your principal residence and is insured for at least 80% of its full rebuilding cost, or for the $250,000 maximum.

What does it cost in my flood zone?

From about $1,062 a year (Zone X) to $1,417 (Zone AE) here. Your zone is on your lender's flood determination or FEMA's map; find its row below.

Flood zoneMedian / yrPriced policies
Zone AE$1,417537

What the zone codes mean (44 CFR §64.3): A, AE and A1–A30 are high-risk; AO and AH are high-risk with shallow flooding; A99 is high-risk behind a flood barrier FEMA treats as complete; V, VE and V1–V30 are coastal high-risk, flooded by tides with fast-moving water (velocity); B and X are areas of moderate flood hazard, C and X areas of minimal hazard; D has possible but undetermined flood hazards. A 1 percent or greater chance a year works out to a 26% or greater chance of at least one such flood over 30 years.

Zones with fewer than 50 priced single-family policies are omitted. Your own premium still depends on elevation and coverage.

How Gulf County appears in the national research papers

Each paper sorts the U.S. counties with enough records by one measure into five groups of about equal size, from highest fifth to lowest fifth. A group is a position in a list, not a grade or a prediction.

  • Flood damage over building coverage: NFIP claims by county: Of 432 paid single-family primary-home claims with recorded damage and coverage here (losses 2016–2025), 7.6% (90% range 5.8–10.0%) had recorded building damage over the building coverage. That ranks in the highest fifth of 268 U.S. counties listed.
  • Outside the zone: paid flood claims rated outside high-risk zones: Of 938 claims with a payment and a rated zone here (losses 2016–2025), 23.6% (90% range 21.4–25.9%) were rated outside zones A and V. That ranks in the middle fifth of 364 U.S. counties listed.
  • Building deductibles on record: NFIP single-family homes by county: Of 802 single-family primary-home policy units with a known building deductible here, 14.6% (90% range 12.7–16.8%) had a building deductible of $5,000 or more on record. That ranks in the second-lowest fifth of 1,793 U.S. counties listed.
  • Peak month of NFIP claims by county: Of 999 NFIP claims with a month of loss here (losses 2016–2025), 96.9% (90% range 95.9–97.7%) were in their county's peak month. That ranks in the highest fifth of 416 U.S. counties listed. Peak month: October, over half of it from October 2018 alone. At random, 9.9% of claims would land in one month at this size, so the ranking uses the share above that.
  • The gap to FEMA's full-risk premium: NFIP single-family homes by county: Of 802 single-family primary-home policies priced both ways here, 50.6% (90% range 47.7–53.5%) had a premium at least $100 a year below FEMA's full-risk premium. That ranks in the highest fifth of 1,793 U.S. counties listed.

How much flood risk is here?

Relatively Moderate for coastal flooding and Very Low for inland (river) flooding, by FEMA's county rating. That compares this county with others; it is not a forecast for your address.

  • Coastal flood risk rating (FEMA)Relatively Moderate
  • Inland flood risk rating (FEMA)Very Low

FEMA's rating weighs modeled loss with social vulnerability and community resilience. It is not a prediction for your home, and it can differ from the loss percentile below. FEMA's model puts yearly flood loss here at roughly $516,792 for coastal flooding and $2.4 million for inland flooding. It counts buildings, people and farmland valued in dollars, insured or not, so it runs far above insurance payouts. A separate FEMA measure, loss per dollar of building value, is higher here than in about 90% of U.S. counties for coastal flooding and about 46% for inland flooding. How this is counted

Source: FEMA — National Risk Index (flood). Data: NRI December 2025 release; retrieved November 14, 2026.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $10.4 million for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $2,327 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Only disasters counted in the flood-disaster card are included; their aid can still cover wind or tornado damage from the same storm. Disasters for COVID, fire, winter storms or tornadoes alone are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved November 14, 2026.
